title: Preterite vs Imperfect in Spanish: When to Use Each
seo_title: Preterite vs Imperfect in Spanish: When to Use Each
meta_description: Preterite vs imperfect in Spanish: the preterite tells what happened, the imperfect sets the scene. Clear rules, story examples and a quick quiz.
excerpt: One tense tells the story; the other paints the background. Here is how Spanish speakers choose.

body_html:
Preterite vs imperfect is the question every Spanish learner meets as soon as they start telling stories. Spanish has two simple past tenses where English mostly has one. The clearest way to see it: the preterite tells you what happened, as completed events, one after another. The imperfect describes what things were like: the background, habits, ongoing actions and descriptions. Llovía cuando salí means “It was raining when I left”: the rain is the scene (imperfect), and leaving is the event (preterite).

Quick answer
  • Preterite (hablé, comí, fui) = completed actions with a clear beginning or end.
  • Imperfect (hablaba, comía, iba) = background, description, habits, “used to” and “was …ing”.
  • In a story: imperfect sets the scene, preterite moves the plot forward.
{{toc}}

Preterite vs imperfect: the core difference

PreteriteImperfect
FocusThe event as a whole, finishedThe middle of an action, or a state
EnglishI spoke, I ate, I wentI was speaking, I used to eat, I would go
Signal wordsayer, anoche, el lunes, una vez, de repentesiempre, todos los días, mientras, de niño, a menudo
ExampleAyer comí tacos. Yesterday I ate tacos.De niño comía tacos cada domingo. As a kid I used to eat tacos every Sunday.

Signal words help, but they are not rules. The real question is always how you see the action: as a finished event, or as something in progress or repeated.

When to use the preterite

  • Completed actions: Terminé el libro anoche. I finished the book last night.
  • A series of events: Me levanté, me bañé y salí. I got up, showered and left.
  • Actions with a defined length: Viví en Texas cinco años. I lived in Texas for five years (and that period is over).
  • An interruption: Sonó el teléfono. The phone rang.
  • The beginning or end of something: Empezó a llover a las tres. It started raining at three.
{{image:2}}

When to use the imperfect

  • Habits in the past (“used to”, “would”): Cada verano íbamos a la playa. Every summer we would go to the beach.
  • Ongoing actions (“was …ing”): Mientras cocinaba, escuchaba música. While I was cooking, I was listening to music.
  • Descriptions of people, places and weather: La casa era pequeña y hacía frío. The house was small and it was cold.
  • Time and age: Eran las ocho. It was eight o’clock. Tenía diez años. I was ten.
  • Feelings and mental states: Estaba nervioso y no sabía qué decir. I was nervous and didn’t know what to say.

How the two work together in a story

Most real stories use both tenses, and the contrast is what makes them work. Read this short example:

Era un sábado por la tarde. Hacía sol y mis hijos jugaban en el jardín. Yo leía en la terraza cuando de repente sonó el timbre. Abrí la puerta y vi a mi hermana. ¡No la esperaba!

The imperfect (era, hacía, jugaban, leía, esperaba) builds the scene. The preterite (sonó, abrí, vi) tells you what happened in it. If you rewrote the whole thing in the preterite, it would sound like a list of facts; all in the imperfect, nothing would ever happen.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Verbs that change meaning

A few verbs change their English translation depending on the tense, because the preterite focuses on a moment and the imperfect on a state.

VerbImperfectPreterite
conocerconocía I knew (someone)conocí I met (for the first time)
sabersabía I knew (a fact)supe I found out
quererquería I wantedno quise I refused
poderpodía I was able to (in general)pude I managed to

For more on the first two, see {{link:saber-vs-conocer|saber vs conocer}}.

Common mistakes

  • Using the preterite for age: Cuando tuve diez años… should be Cuando tenía diez años…
  • Using the imperfect for a one-time event: Ayer iba al médico. should be Ayer fui al médico.
  • Forgetting the imperfect for habits: De niño jugué al béisbol cada día. should be jugaba.

The Centro Virtual Cervantes has free grammar resources if you want more practice with the forms themselves.

{{image:3}}

Practice: tell your own story

The best practice is personal. Think of a small event from last week, like a dinner, a trip to the store or a phone call. First, describe the scene in the imperfect: what time it was, where you were, what the weather was like, how you felt and what people were doing. Then tell what happened in the preterite, one event after another.

For example: Eran las siete. Estaba en la cocina y mi esposo veía la tele. De repente, se fue la luz. Encendimos unas velas y cenamos juntos en la terraza. It was seven o’clock. I was in the kitchen and my husband was watching TV. Suddenly the power went out. We lit some candles and had dinner together on the terrace.

Write three or four of these mini stories. Read them aloud. Within a couple of weeks, the rhythm of scene and event starts to feel natural, and that is when the choice stops being a grammar question.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Preterite vs imperfect is less about rules and more about perspective. Ask yourself whether you are telling what happened or describing how things were. Read stories in Spanish and notice how the two tenses take turns, and soon the choice will feel natural. For the other pairs that confuse learners, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between the preterite and the imperfect?
faq.a: The preterite presents past actions as completed events. The imperfect describes ongoing actions, habits, descriptions, time and age in the past.
Imperfect: Yo jugaba al fútbol means “I used to play soccer”.

faq.q: Do I use preterite or imperfect for age?
faq.a: The imperfect: Tenía veinte años cuando me mudé. I was twenty when I moved.

faq.q: Can a sentence use both tenses?
faq.a: Yes, and very often. Leía cuando llegaste combines an ongoing action (imperfect) with an event that interrupts it (preterite).
